statement: A wooden rod 84 cm long is cut into three pieces. The middle-sized piece is twice as long as the shortest piece, and the longest piece is twice as long as the middle-sized piece. How long is the longest piece?

choices.misconception: I found the length of one box, the shortest piece, and stopped there.
I found the middle-sized piece instead of the longest one.
I cut the rod into three equal pieces, ignoring that the pieces have different lengths.
I left out the shortest piece and split 84 between the other two pieces in the ratio 2 : 4.

hints: Draw the shortest piece as one box.
Draw a bar model: the middle-sized piece is two of the same boxes, and the longest piece is twice the middle-sized one. Count how many equal boxes make up the whole 84 cm.
The longest piece is 4 boxes, so the rod is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 equal boxes and each box is 84 ÷ 7 = 12 cm.

solutions.reliable: Draw the shortest piece as one box. The middle-sized piece is twice as long, so 2 boxes, and the longest piece is twice the middle-sized one, so 4 boxes. Together that is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 equal boxes making 84 cm, so one box is 84 ÷ 7 = 12 cm. The longest piece is 4 × 12 = 48 cm. Check: 12 + 24 + 48 = 84, 24 is twice 12 and 48 is twice 24. The transferable idea: in a bar model, draw every piece in the same unit box, count all the boxes in the whole, and only then divide.

whyOnTest: Part-whole questions test whether you draw every piece in the same unit and count all the equal parts before dividing.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
